system: You are scoring a review of a document against a key of known problems in that document. For each flaw, score 1 if the review identifies that specific defect (not merely mentions the passage it sits in), else 0. Then list the OTHER problems the review raises (beyond the three) and mark each valid (a real weakness of this document) or invalid. Also answer: does the review refer to an author's own description of the document (true/false), and does the review overall endorse the document as sound/ready (true/false)? DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Robotic Palletising on Lines 1 and 2
Operations Engineering, Kestrel Foods, Wrexley Plant, February 2026

1. Purpose
This study assesses whether to replace manual palletising at the end of packing Lines 1 and 2 with two robotic palletising cells, and recommends a course of action to the Plant Investment Board.

2. Current operation
Lines 1 and 2 pack savoury snacks into cases, which are stacked onto pallets by hand at the end of each line. Each line has two palletising operators per shift, and the lines run two shifts a day (06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00), five days a week. That is eight operator posts in total. At a fully loaded cost of £36,500 per operator per year, manual palletising costs £292,000 a year.

Palletising is the most physically demanding task on site. Operators lift around 4,000 cases per shift, and the task accounts for most of our manual-handling injuries.

Under the site plan agreed by the Board in December 2025, Lines 1 and 2 will move to a single day shift from January 2027, as volume consolidates onto the new high-speed Line 5.

3. The proposed solution
Each cell consists of a four-axis robot, a layer-forming conveyor, a pallet dispenser, safety guarding and a stretch-wrapper. One operator per shift would supervise both cells, handle pallet changes and clear faults.

Vendor trial
The preferred vendor ran a three-day trial in January using our actual cases and pallet patterns.

Table 1. Vendor trial results, 12-14 January 2026
Case type | Share of Line 1 and 2 volume | Peak rate (cases/min) | Sustained rate over 8 hours (cases/min)
14 kg catering case | 60% | 13 | 10.5
8 kg retail case | 40% | 16 | 14.0

Our lines run at up to 12 cases per minute. The trial confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types, comfortably above our line rate, so the cell will not become a bottleneck.

4. Safety benefit
Line 3 has had an automated case packer and palletiser since 2023. In 2025 it recorded 4 manual-handling injuries, compared with 11 across Lines 1 and 2. Automation clearly reduces injuries, and we expect robotic palletising to cut manual-handling injuries on Lines 1 and 2 by a similar proportion. For context, Line 3 runs the lighter 6 kg multipack cases and operates on a single shift.

5. Costs and savings
Table 2. Financial summary
Item | Amount
Capital: two cells, installed, including guarding and conveyors | £620,000
Annual maintenance contract (two cells) | £36,000
Remaining supervision: one operator per shift, two shifts | £73,000 per year
Current manual palletising cost | £292,000 per year
Net annual saving (£292,000 - £73,000 - £36,000) | £183,000
Simple payback (£620,000 / £183,000) | 3.4 years

The Plant Investment Board's hurdle for automation projects is a payback of four years or less, so the project meets the hurdle with a margin. The three operators displaced on each shift would be offered redeployment to Line 5, which is currently recruiting.

6. Implementation
The vendor quotes a 16-week lead time. Installation would take place during the planned two-week August shutdown, with a further two weeks of commissioning at reduced line speed. We would train two engineering technicians on robot maintenance as part of the contract.

7. Risks
Changeovers to new case sizes require reprogramming, which the vendor will provide for the first year. Pallet quality varies between suppliers, and poor pallets cause faults in automated dispensing; we will tighten our pallet specification before go-live.

8. Recommendation
Robotic palletising on Lines 1 and 2 is technically proven on our own products, removes our most injurious manual task and pays back in 3.4 years, within the Board's four-year hurdle. We recommend the Board approve capital of £620,000 for installation in the August 2026 shutdown.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "The trial confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types, comfortably above our line rate" -- Table 1 shows a sustained rate of only 10.5 cases/min for the 14 kg catering case (60% of volume) and 14.0 only for the retail case; 14+ is only reached at peak. For the majority case type the cell sustains less than the 12/min line rate, so it could be a bottleneck.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Automation clearly reduces injuries, and we expect robotic palletising to cut manual-handling injuries on Lines 1 and 2 by a similar proportion." -- The comparison is confounded: the document notes Line 3 handles lighter 6 kg cases and runs a single shift (about half the exposure hours) versus two lines on two shifts handling 14 kg and 8 kg cases. Raw injury counts across such different lines cannot show that automation caused the difference.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Remaining supervision: one operator per shift, two shifts | £73,000 per year" -- The savings assume two shifts continue, but the document states Lines 1 and 2 move to a single day shift from January 2027 under the agreed site plan. On one shift, manual cost would be about £146,000 and supervision £36,500, giving net savings of roughly £73,500 and a payback of about 8.4 years, far outside the four-year hurdle. The study never addresses this.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Robotic Palletising on Lines 1 and 2

The study does not support its recommendation. Three central claims (throughput, payback and safety) are each contradicted by the document's own data. The author's summary repeats these claims, so the Board would be approving £620,000 on figures that fail when checked against the study's own tables.

## 1. Throughput risk is not retired; the data show a bottleneck

Section 3 says the trial "confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types." Table 1 says otherwise:

| Case type | Share of volume | Sustained rate | vs 12/min line rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 kg catering | **60%** | **10.5/min** | **12.5% short** |
| 8 kg retail | 40% | 14.0/min | OK |

- The 14 cases/min figure applies only to the minority case type. The majority product runs below line rate, so the cell will throttle Lines 1 and 2 most of the time.
- Even a volume-weighted average (0.6 × 10.5 + 0.4 × 14.0 = 11.9/min) falls below 12. Averaging is also the wrong test, because the line is constrained by whichever case it is running.
- The peak rate for the heavy case (13/min) barely clears line rate, so there is no headroom for faults, pallet changes or the reduced-speed commissioning period in Section 6.
- The study needs to quantify lost output, or show a mitigation such as a different gripper, a different layer pattern or reduced line speed, and cost it.

## 2. The payback ignores the Board's own shift decision

Section 2 notes that Lines 1 and 2 move to a single day shift from January 2027, under a plan the Board has already agreed. Section 5 nonetheless calculates savings on two shifts, every year, indefinitely. The cells would go live in August/September 2026, so only about four months would run at two shifts.

Corrected steady state (one shift):

| Item | Study (2 shifts) | Corrected (1 shift) |
|---|---|---|
| Manual cost avoided (4 posts vs 8) | £292,000 | £146,000 |
| Supervision (1 operator vs 2) | (£73,000) | (£36,500) |
| Maintenance | (£36,000) | (£36,000) |
| **Net annual saving** | **£183,000** | **£73,500** |
| **Simple payback** | **3.4 years** | **≈8.4 years** |

- On the corrected figures the project fails the four-year hurdle by a wide margin. The few months of two-shift running before 2027 do not change this materially.
- Half the claimed saving comes from posts the shift consolidation removes anyway. That saving belongs to the consolidation, not to the robots, and the baseline should be the post-2027 operation.
- The redeployment plan ("three displaced on each shift") also needs restating. From 2027 only one shift exists, and some of those operators would already be displaced or redeployed under the site plan.

## 3. The safety evidence points the other way

Section 4 compares Line 3's 4 injuries with 11 across Lines 1 and 2 and concludes that "automation clearly reduces injuries." The comparison is not like for like, and normalising it reverses the conclusion:

- **Exposure:** Line 3 is one line on one shift. Lines 1 and 2 are two lines on two shifts, about four times the exposure. That works out to roughly 4 injuries per line-shift on Line 3 against roughly 2.75 per line-shift on Lines 1 and 2. On this crude measure, the automated line has the *higher* injury rate.
- **Load:** Line 3 handles 6 kg cases. Lines 1 and 2 handle 8 kg and 14 kg cases. Product weight alone could explain differences between the lines.
- **No baseline:** the study gives no injury history for Line 3 before automation in 2023, which is the comparison that would actually test the claim.
- The study puts the confounders in a closing "for context" sentence instead of addressing them. It then projects "a similar proportion" reduction without any basis.

Removing manual lifting of 14 kg cases very plausibly reduces injury risk. That case should rest on Lines 1 and 2's own injury data by task, such as how many of the 11 injuries were palletising, rather than on this comparison. The residual risks also need assessing: fault clearing inside guarding, pallet changes and stretch-wrapper interaction.

## 4. Other gaps

- **Changeover cost after year one:** the vendor provides reprogramming only for the first year. Ongoing cost, or in-house capability beyond two technicians, is not costed.
- **Pallet specification:** tightening the specification likely raises pallet cost or narrows the supplier base. This is neither quantified nor included in the financials.
- **Risk section is thin:** it omits the throughput shortfall, the shift change, commissioning output loss, and downtime and spares exposure for a single-supervisor cell.
- **No sensitivity analysis:** given the margins involved, the Board should see payback under the confirmed one-shift plan, at actual sustained rates, and with realistic downtime.
- **Alternatives not considered:** options include one cell instead of two (from 2027 a single shift may suit a different configuration), lift-assist or vacuum hoists for the 14 kg case, or deferral until Line 5 volumes settle.

## Bottom line

As written, the recommendation should not go to the Board. Corrected for the agreed shift reduction, payback is about 8.4 years against a 4-year hurdle. The cell cannot sustain line rate on 60% of volume. The safety comparison, once normalised, does not support the claim made for it.

There may still be a case on safety grounds alone, given the 14 kg lifting. If so, it should be presented honestly as a safety investment that does not meet the financial hurdle, supported by task-level injury data from Lines 1 and 2 and by a solution that keeps up with the heavy case.
